title: Vibe coding Metal Gear Rising
author: Ssabsucitivel
selftext: Do you y'all think it's possible. MGR is one of my favorite games because of the slomo chopping. I'm seriously considering buying a PC and trying to make my dream game with this same "zandatsu" chopping gameplay. I've been talking to Chat GPT and Claude about the feasibility of this and they both think it's going to be very difficult. But I still want to try. Nanomachines son.

comments.author: yaosio
comments.body:
Making a single feature is much easier than making an entire game. If your only idea is Metal Gear Rising, but newer, it's just going to be a direct clone of Metal Gear Rising. Is it only the chopping mechanic that you like where you can chop things up? You don't need to remake an existing game for that, you could make a new game, a smaller game, based around just that mechanic and interesting things you could do with it or add onto it.

If you want to have some real fun do all your vibecoding via the respective apps. I've done everything on a software toy I'm working on via the Claude app on mobile in Claude Code. Although what I'm making is strictly 2D.

comments.author: sevenoutdb
comments.body:
I'm sorry to tell you this, and I honestly mean no malice. You are not going to get to a quality game unless you invest months and months in setting up this game and devise an entire 3D character pipeline (concept art, modeling, texturing, rigging, animation, and THEN game programming). You will need adapt a very complex melee combat system (for "zandatsu") and on top of all of this, you need to make the game worth playing beyond the prototype combat scene. You need a story, dialogue, characters/enemies, environments, props, a progression system, inventory system, all of that.

HOWEVER, if you can come up with a way to make this work in a 2D game, you'd have a much better chance at coming out the other side... and you could have a compelling game experience too. I would maybe ask ChatGPT or Claude if they have any ideas on how that could work, and of course, you need to add your own theme and spin. More sci-fi, more fantasy? more cyberpunk? Grimdark? Maybe a parody/comedy version?

replies.author: Ssabsucitivel
replies.body: Well my game idea is to  be a faux multiplayer.  You play against bots. No progression, no inventory, no story, one single environment. You spawn into a city level and have 15 minutes to get as many kills as possible. As for my take on "zandatsu" you will create a forcefield bubble and an enemy trapped in the bubble gets slo-moed and you can chop them their sheild  is broken. And I'm also not going to have parrying. Or even other sword attacks, all of your attacks will be projectile shooting except for the zandatsu

replies.author: sevenoutdb
replies.body:
Okay, I think I get it. From what you are saying, you are going to try to build one environment, and base the gameplay around a core combat mechanic. Many games have been made around a core gameplay mechanic and then the rest of the game structure was emergent gameplay. (A lot of this in VR games and early mobile touchscreen games) 

Obviously you can do whatever you want in game dev, it just takes time and creativity, but I will also tell you that you should not ignore the need for a metagame or basically no one will play the game more than a few time, because aside from more kills in less time, there’s nothing to work towards, nothing to unlock, no reward for the time they’ve invested.

comments.author: Relevant-Positive-48
comments.body:
First off, I really hope you're looking to make a game inspired by Metal Gear Rising and not planning to violate tradmark/copyright.  However you might feel about trademarks and copyright you're asking for a world of trouble if you infringe them.

Second, yeah, it's pretty much possible to vibe code (by vibe code I mean using a wide variety of AI tools without being an expert in them, you'll need way more than code) anything these days but don't expect a production ready game of the scale and quality of something like Metal Gear Rising to be quick.  You'll get fooled by the fast, easy and impressive looking progress early and underestimate how much work goes into making it good.  (Incidentally this isn't new to the AI era, cool looking prototypes were always much faster than the complete game - how many times did we see a super cool demo and then had to wait 3 years for the game to be done).

replies.author: Ssabsucitivel
replies.body: Yes I'm going to violate trademark/copyright 💀

comments.author: TheReviewerWildTake
comments.body:
Tbh I would rather start with modding some existing games and see how it goes on in a smaller scope.  
  
It would give you a more compact view on specific challenges of combat animations, and then you can take that foundation to a brand new game.  
  
There is almost 99% probability that your fully vibecoded MGR gonna play like crap and will be abandoned.   
That is just sad statistics of this kind of ambitious starts.   
Because AI is deceptively powerful at certain things, but then you run into a field where it is helpless, and then people without experience just fold, because at this point there is no way to salvage it - as the project is just too huge and complex, and looks incredibly intimidating and messy to work with.   
  
You really don\`t want to get into late game development stage as a total vibe-coding newbie who has no idea on what is going on in the codebase. It will be super disheartening.  
There is a reason why overwhelming majority of "tech-demos" you see on this sub and other AI centric subs  - are abandoned and you never hear about them after.

comments.author: zenmatrix83
comments.body: the coding part is easier then the art, and it will take alot of time even with ai, no ai can make a full game of that level. Small basic tech demos are currently  what are being made, some look good and copy real games but are just basic imidations of smaller parts.
